summary_html: Immediate state action to **protect a child in imminent danger**. Federal law (ASFA/IV-E) ties funding to court findings on **reasonable efforts**, and constitutional limits (due process, 4th/14th Amendments) constrain warrantless removals.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — reasonable-efforts findings; permanency timelines  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal oversight of removal decision quality  
- **Constitutional constraints** — enforced via §1983 actions; due process & search/seizure jurisprudence (not listed in file but governs practice)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
key_cases.holding: Triable issues existed on the parents' procedural due process claim and the child's Fourth Amendment unreasonable-seizure claim arising from her removal from school without a court order, although the defendants retained qualified immunity because the rule was not clearly established in 1990.
key_cases.relevance: Tenenbaum is the governing Second Circuit rule for Vermont on when protective custody may be taken without prior judicial authorization.
key_cases.quote: where there is reasonable time consistent with the safety of the child to obtain a judicial order, the “emergency” removal of a child is unwarranted

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
key_cases.holding: Agency lawyers who initiate and prosecute child-protective proceedings have absolute immunity from § 1983 claims, but caseworkers do not, because their removal decisions are the functional equivalent of an arrest; on these facts the caseworkers were nevertheless protected by qualified immunity.
key_cases.relevance: It confirms that the official who takes a child into protective custody is subject to the ordinary objective-reasonableness test rather than absolute immunity.
key_cases.quote: The caseworker defendants are not entitled to absolute immunity on plaintiffs § 1983 claims because their actions were the functional equivalent of arresting officers in criminal cases.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
key_cases.holding: Summary judgment for the defendants was affirmed because during the relevant period the newborn was held by the hospital for medical reasons rather than by the child-welfare agency, so no Fourth or Fourteenth Amendment violation arose from the retention.
key_cases.relevance: It shows that not every hospital retention of a child amounts to a state seizure triggering protective-custody analysis.
key_cases.quote: Mora was held by the Hospital for medical reasons, not concerns about possible parental mistreatment and CWA policies

key_cases.holding: A post-disposition order transferring custody of a child back to DCF is a final appealable order, and the preponderance standard, not clear and convincing evidence, governs it because the deprivation is temporary rather than a permanent severance.
key_cases.relevance: I.B. distinguishes the lower proof required for temporary state custody from the clear and convincing showing required for permanent severance.
key_cases.quote: In its decision to modify the plan to transfer legal custody of I.B. back to DCF, therefore, the trial court here applied the proper standard of proof.

key_cases.case_name: Southerland v. City of New York
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
key_cases.holding: Summary judgment for the caseworker was vacated on the Fourth Amendment unlawful-search claims arising from a family-court entry order obtained through allegedly false statements, on the procedural due process claims, and on the children's Fourth Amendment unlawful-seizure claim, because qualified immunity could not be resolved as a matter of law on that record; summary judgment was affirmed only on the father's substantive due process claim.
key_cases.relevance: Southerland is the leading modern Second Circuit statement, binding in Vermont, that a child may not be taken into protective custody absent a court order, parental consent, or genuine emergency circumstances.
key_cases.quote: the Children's right not to be taken from the care of their parent without court order, parental consent, or emergency circumstances was firmly established

search_keywords: Vermont Department for Children and Families

state_agency.name: Vermont Department for Children and Families, Family Services Division

mandatory_reporters: Health care providers, including physicians, surgeons, osteopaths, chiropractors, physician assistants, resident physicians, interns, hospital administrators, registered nurses, licensed practical nurses, medical examiners, emergency medical personnel, dentists, psychologists, and pharmacists — 33 V.S.A. § 4913(a)(1)

School district and approved or recognized independent school employees, and contracted student-services providers, including superintendents, headmasters, teachers, student teachers, school librarians, principals, and guidance counselors — 33 V.S.A. § 4913(a)(2)
Agency of Human Services employees, contractors, and grantees who have contact with clients — 33 V.S.A. § 4913(a)(7)
Camp owners (“camp” includes any residential or nonresidential recreational program, 33 V.S.A. § 4913(b)) — 33 V.S.A. § 4913(a)(9)
Members of the clergy, except information received while acting as a spiritual advisor in a confidential communication (33 V.S.A. § 4913(j)) — 33 V.S.A. § 4913(a)(12)
Employees of the Office of the Child, Youth, and Family Advocate — 33 V.S.A. § 4913(a)(13)
reporting_details: Vermont is not a universal-reporting state: the 13 categories of mandated reporters listed in 33 V.S.A. § 4913(a) must report to DCF within 24 hours of the time the information was first received or observed, and any other concerned person may report voluntarily (33 V.S.A. § 4913(c), (e)).

timeline_requirements.deadline: 72 hours to begin an assessment or investigation
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Receipt of the report, once accepted as a valid allegation and there is sufficient information to proceed
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: The Commissioner may waive the 72-hour requirement only when necessary to locate the child or to ensure the safety of the child or social worker (33 V.S.A. § 4915(b)).

timeline_requirements.deadline: 45 days (assessment track); no statutory deadline (investigation track)
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: An assessment may be extended only upon written justification by the Department and not beyond 60 days total (33 V.S.A. § 4915a(b)); Vermont sets no completion deadline for the investigation track (33 V.S.A. § 4915b).
